chapter: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
title: Boston saxophonists Eric Brown, Don Pasquale and Benny Waters
summary: He recalls the conservatory-trained Eric Brown, teacher Don Pasquale, and the showman Benny Waters compared with sedentary Hodges.

blocks.x: There was another saxophonist by the name of Eric Brown.

Eric Brown. Couldn't tell you too much about him except that he was a hell of a saxophone player, and fast as lightning, and clean as can be. He was a conservatory graduate. Like, he came to Boston to study at the Conservatory.
And then, I understand, so did Don Pasquale.
So he also, then, was someone who from time to time
would give pointers on the instrument?
Well, Brownie possibly, but Pasquale certainly.

Well, Pasquale, he went in and he was teaching. He was teaching up there. Yeah, he was teaching quite a few of the boys. I never heard... Let me see. At that time, I couldn't afford to pay for the lessons. It was hard enough for my Daddy to pay for the saxophone without the lessons.
And then also in Boston you met Benny Waters.
Yeah. He came up here to go to school and play music at the Conservatory.
So that was still another way of playing the saxophone that you heard.

Oh yeah, he could play, too. Very good. Very-very-very good. And he was a salesman with it, too. He could sell what he was doing. He wasn't no Johnny Hodges, sitting up there looking like he was going to sleep! (Don't put that in. Please don't put that in.)
No, well, don't put that in there from me, because Cue will be giving me... She calls me every week, you know. Oh, she'll be giving me hell about that.
But anyway, he was a live-wire and he...

Oh, then he was playin' and hoppin' around and... he was selling it, you know! He was selling himself. See, Johnny would get up there and play, but he... Thing is, he wouldn't even stand up when he played a solo. He'd sit down. Sit down, cross his legs, play. But he was playin'. No salesmanship.
